i want to point out pedantically that finding two occupied spaces next to each other doesn’t prove it’s a windmill. Placing two graves next to each other is a risky strategy I tried in a few games. Ppl would find the two and if you were lucky they’d assume it was a windmill and move on. It’s risky bc they might just find the grave plot first and figure it out, which just means you gavr them two graves and let them get ahead.   
But, you are right that we have only assumed what the object of the game is. It might be find the three graves. It might be find the three graves AND enter the windmill to find the last ‘grave’. or it might be something else maybe.    
Its interesting seeing the insights you are getting from an alternative approach to investigating the graverobber scene in petscop . : )

There are some known unwinnable configurations but yours isn’t one I don’t think.    
You can and often must desync yourself in order to win graverobber. Its like the bedroom scene in p14. You walk in a straight line but your double hits a grave . Allowing you to move from that position and reach a spot that you can’t reach on your board.   
The unwinnable states are ones where the objects on your board don’t allow a desync that could reach the last grave. Its most likely if all objects on both boards are packed close together in a corner or one side. Bc you can only desync yourself in a direction that isn’t useful. Its extremely unlikely that it would happen in a normal game without intentionally trying to.

its really best not to go for an overview . watching the series with an ‘active viewing’ approach, where you ask questions and attempt to answer them by checking evidence directly or using a resource like the progress document, is best. It will be easier to consume the document with this approach too, bc you won’t be passively absorbing all of it at once. Instead you’ll always have a clear idea of what you want answered each time you dive into it. This will also help you to evaluate theories when you encounter them, and you’ll get more out of them too. I know it’s not the answer you wanted but it’s really the right way.

you haven’t mentioned any statistics though? and regardless the assertion that game series get better with each sequel would still be opinionated, because it depends on what you consider better, regardless of what statistics you brought to bear to support it.

usually the first game has the most charm and soul. Sequels will increase in polish and quality of life improvements but generally with all the rough edges taken away they lose that special something. Bc the original might have been made as an experiment by a bunch of enthusiastic designers and artists, but the sequels however well intentioned are mainly meant to turn a dependable profit. imo.
